titre: Network and Protocol · IPv4, IPv6, Subnetting & Protocols
matiere: Ch1 Addressing · Ch2 IPv4 · Ch3 Subnetting · Ch4 IPv6 · Ch5 Switching · Ch6 Routing · Ch7 Transport & Application

questions.question: Who assigns the manufacturer (MFG) code of a Layer 2 address to each vendor?
questions.explication: Layer 2 addresses have two parts: the MFG code, assigned to each vendor by the IEEE, and a unique identifier assigned by the vendor to each board.
questions.piege: The ITU is a classic distractor: it does not assign MAC vendor codes.

questions.question: Who assigns the unique identifier part of a MAC address?
choix: The vendor that produces the board
The IEEE for every single device
The DHCP server of the LAN
questions.explication: The IEEE gives the vendor its code; the vendor then assigns a unique identifier to each board it produces.

questions.question: How is the Layer 2 address space described in the course?
choix: Hierarchical, with network and host parts
Local, unique only inside one subnet
questions.explication: Layer 2 addresses assume a flat address space with universally unique addresses.

questions.question: Who generally determines Layer 3 addresses?
questions.explication: Layer 3 addresses are determined by the network administrator, who installs a hierarchy on the network.

questions.question: A user moves to another building. What happens to the end station's addresses?
choix: New Layer 3 address, same Layer 2 address
New Layer 2 address, same Layer 3 address
questions.explication: If users move to another building, their end stations obtain new Layer 3 addresses, but their Layer 2 addresses remain the same.

questions.question: Which Protocol Data Unit (PDU) does a Layer 2 switch usually forward?
questions.explication: Switches use Layer 2 switching to forward frames, based on MAC address information.
questions.piege: Packet = Layer 3 (routers), segment = Layer 4 (TCP). A Layer 2 switch forwards frames.

questions.question: What information does a router use to forward a packet?
choix: The source port number of the segment
The destination MAC address in the frame
The VLAN tag carried by the frame
questions.explication: Layer 3 switching (routing) forwards packets based on their network-layer destination addresses.

questions.question: What does a Layer 2 switch do with a frame whose destination MAC address is not in its table?
choix: It forwards it to the default gateway
It sends the frame back to the source
It floods the frame out of all its ports
questions.explication: If the switch does not know where to send the frame, it broadcasts it out all its ports, then learns the location from the reply.

questions.question: How does a switch learn which MAC address is on which port?
choix: By reading the destination address of each frame
By reading the source address of each frame
questions.explication: The switch looks at the source address of incoming frames and builds its switching table from it.

questions.question: In the course's definitions, what does a 'route' identify?
questions.explication: A name identifies what you want, an address where it is, and a route a way to get there.

questions.question: Host 129.99.0.1/16 sends to 136.178.0.1/16. What must exist between them?
choix: A hub on the same segment
questions.explication: Devices on other networks can only be reached through a router connecting the networks.

questions.question: What does hierarchical routing mean?
choix: Only one router is allowed per site
questions.explication: In hierarchical routing, knowledge of the topology is localized: no single router needs to know how to reach every other segment.

questions.question: Packet from PC1 (192.168.10.10) to PC2 (192.168.20.10) via R1 and R2. Which addresses does it carry when it reaches R2's interface?
questions.explication: Without NAT, source and destination IP addresses stay the same end to end; only the MAC addresses change at each hop.
questions.piege: Do not replace the IPs by the router interfaces' addresses: only Layer 2 addresses are rewritten.

questions.question: A LAN must be connected to the Internet through a leased line. What is the minimum device needed?
choix: A router with two Ethernet interfaces
A router with one Ethernet and one modem interface
A switch with one Ethernet and one serial interface
A router with one Ethernet and one serial interface
questions.explication: Joining two networks needs a router; the leased line connects to a serial (WAN) interface and the LAN to an Ethernet interface.

questions.question: How many bits does an IPv4 address have?
questions.explication: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four octets in dotted decimal notation.

questions.question: Which class does an address whose first octet is 172 belong to?
questions.explication: Class B covers first octets 128 to 191.

questions.question: Which first-octet range corresponds to class C?
questions.explication: Class C addresses start with bits 110, i.e. first octet 192 to 223, prefix length 24.

questions.question: What are class D addresses (224 to 239) used for?
questions.explication: Class D (first bits 1110) is reserved for IP multicast.

questions.question: What are addresses starting with 127 reserved for?
choix: IP traffic local to a host
questions.explication: Addresses starting with 127 are reserved for IP traffic local to a host (loopback).

questions.question: Which address type refers to a group of hosts?
questions.explication: Unicast = single machine, multicast = group of hosts, broadcast = all local hosts.
questions.piege: Broadcast is ALL local hosts, not a group. Anycast belongs to IPv6.

questions.question: Which address type reaches all local hosts?
questions.explication: A broadcast address reaches all local hosts.

questions.question: For the IP address 130.100.50.100, what is the maximum number of usable host addresses?
questions.explication: 130 is class B: 16 host bits, so 2^16 - 2 = 65,534 usable hosts.
questions.piege: 65,536 forgets to remove the network and broadcast addresses.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses does a class C network have?
questions.explication: 8 host bits: 2^8 - 2 = 254.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses does a class A network have?
Why do we subtract two when counting the hosts of a network?
choix: All zeros = network, all ones = broadcast
The first and last octets are reserved
Two addresses are kept for the routers
All zeros = gateway, all ones = DNS server
questions.explication: The host part all zeros names the network itself; all ones is the broadcast address.

questions.question: What is the first-bit pattern of a class B address?
questions.explication: Class A starts with 0, B with 10, C with 110, D with 1110, E with 1111.

questions.question: What does the dotted decimal notation do?
choix: Makes the binary address easier to read
Adds the subnet mask to the address
questions.explication: The human mind finds binary hard to memorize; dotted decimal notation makes an IP address easier to read.

questions.question: Convert 10000000 00001011 00000011 00011111 to dotted decimal.
What problem do the Net ID and Host ID alone leave?
questions.explication: Classful addressing gives only two levels (network, host), which is a problem for privacy, security and huge networks; subnetting adds a level.

questions.question: What does the Net ID show?
choix: The port used by the application
The location of a node in the network
The network's location on the Internet
The manufacturer of the network card
questions.explication: The NetID shows the network's location on the Internet; the HostID shows the node within the network.

questions.question: What is the broadcast address of the class A network 10.0.0.0?
questions.explication: All 24 host bits set to 1 give 10.255.255.255. 10.255.255.254 is the last usable host.
questions.piege: One slide writes 10.0.0.255: that would only be right for a /24.

questions.question: Who created the standard subnet masks around 1983?
questions.explication: Standard subnet masks were created by the central Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) around 1983.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of subnetting a corporate network?
questions.explication: Subnetting improves address allocation, performance (smaller broadcast domains) and security. Traffic diversion is not a benefit listed.

questions.question: Which statement about subnetting is FALSE?
choix: It applies a mask to extract the subnet address
It adds another level of hierarchy to a network
It creates private networks with tags and MAC addresses
It segments networks that share internetworking resources
questions.explication: Tagging frames with MAC addresses describes VLANs (Layer 2), not subnetting.
questions.piege: Do not mix up VLAN tagging (Layer 2) and subnetting (Layer 3).

questions.question: What does a subnet mask specify?
choix: Which bits are network/subnet and which are host
Which port number the host is listening on
Which address class the IP address belongs to
Which router is used as the default gateway
questions.explication: The mask specifies which part of an IP address is the network/subnet field and which part is the host field.

questions.question: In binary, what is the prefix portion of a subnet mask made of?
questions.explication: The prefix portion of the mask is all 1s, the host portion all 0s.

questions.question: Which bitwise operation between an address and its mask gives the subnet address?
questions.explication: Address AND mask keeps the bits where the mask is 1: 129.99.30.4 AND 255.255.240.0 = 129.99.16.0.
questions.piege: A slide shows XOR: the correct operation is AND.

questions.question: 129.99.30.4 with mask 255.255.240.0 is on which subnet?
Which prefix length corresponds to 255.255.255.0?
questions.explication: The prefix length is the number of 1s up front: 3 x 8 = 24.

questions.question: Which mask corresponds to /20?
For the class C mask 255.255.255.240, what does the course table give?
questions.explication: 240 = 11110000: 4 borrowed bits give 16 subnets, 4 host bits give 16 addresses per subnet (14 usable).
questions.piege: The slide counts 16 'hosts' = addresses. In a calculation, usable hosts = 16 - 2 = 14.

questions.question: How many usable hosts does a /30 subnet provide?
questions.explication: /30 leaves 2 host bits: 2^2 - 2 = 2. That is why /30 is used for router-to-router links.

questions.question: An engineer must configure a /30 subnet between two routers. Which combination is valid?
questions.explication: In /30 blocks of 4, 209.165.201.2 is a usable host. 10.2.1.3 is a broadcast; .248 is a /29 mask.
questions.piege: The last address of a /30 block (.3, .7, .11...) is the broadcast, never a host.

questions.question: What is the network address of 192.168.10.75/27?
What is the broadcast address of 192.168.10.75/27?
questions.explication: The subnet is .64 to .95: broadcast = next subnet (.96) minus 1 = .95.

questions.question: How many usable hosts are there in a /27 subnet?
questions.explication: 5 host bits: 2^5 - 2 = 30.

questions.question: Splitting 172.16.0.0/16 with a /20 mask gives how many subnets?
questions.explication: 20 - 16 = 4 borrowed bits: 2^4 = 16 subnets.

questions.question: With 172.16.0.0 split into /20 subnets, what is the last usable address of the first subnet?
questions.explication: Block 16 in the third octet: first subnet 172.16.0.0 to 172.16.15.255; last host 172.16.15.254.

questions.question: How many hosts does each /20 subnet of 172.16.0.0 hold?
Which formula gives the number of subnets?
choix: 2 times the number of borrowed bits
2 to the power of host bits, minus 2
The number of host bits squared
2 to the power of the borrowed bits
questions.explication: Number of subnets = 2^(subnet bits); number of hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2.
questions.piege: A slide prints '2 X bits': read it as 2 to the power of the bits.

questions.question: When several routing entries match a destination, which one does the router use?
choix: The first entry in the table
The one whose mask has the fewest 1s
The one whose mask has the most 1s
The entry with the lowest address
questions.explication: The router chooses the entry with the mask with the most ones that matches the destination (longest match).

questions.question: What defines a contiguous subnet mask?
choix: Every one of its octets is either 0 or 255
No 1 bit appears to the right of any 0 bit
No 0 bit appears anywhere in the last octet
It has exactly as many 1 bits as 0 bits
questions.explication: A contiguous mask has all its 1s up front: no 1 bit to the right of a 0 bit.

questions.question: Why can non-contiguous subnet masks be dangerous?
choix: They are refused by every IP stack
Routers may choose different masks and loop
They waste half of the address space
They cannot be written in dotted decimal
questions.explication: Two non-contiguous masks with the same number of ones can both match; IP does not say which to use, so two routers may disagree and create a routing loop.

questions.question: What does a subnet address of all ones mean?
questions.explication: Node all ones = broadcast, node all zeros = network, subnet all ones = all subnets, subnet all zeros = confusing.

questions.question: Which Cisco IOS command permits a subnet address of all zeros?
questions.explication: Cisco IOS permits a subnet address of all zeros with the ip subnet-zero command.

questions.question: Most obvious advantage of VLSM over FLSM?
choix: Load balancing traffic to the WAN
questions.explication: VLSM gives each subnet a mask that fits its size, so it is less wasteful and optimizes the address space.

questions.question: What does VLSM stand for?
questions.explication: VLSM = Variable Length Subnet Mask: a different mask for the same network number on different subnets.

questions.question: Which is NOT another name for route summarization in the course?
questions.explication: Summarization is also called aggregation, supernetting, classless routing, CIDR or prefix routing. Subnetting is the opposite operation.

questions.question: Classless routing protocols do all of the following EXCEPT:
choix: Transmit the prefix length of an IP address
Group networks into one entry with a prefix
Calculate the prefix length from the first bits
questions.explication: Deducing the prefix from the first bits (the class) is what classful routing does.
questions.piege: Read 'EXCEPT' carefully: the odd one out is the classful behaviour.

questions.question: How did classful routing know the prefix length?
choix: From the mask sent in updates
From the class in the first bits
questions.explication: Classful routing did not transmit the prefix length; it was calculated from the address class given by the first few bits.

questions.question: With VLSM, which mask should a LAN of 50 hosts receive?
questions.explication: /26 gives 2^6 - 2 = 62 hosts, the smallest block that fits 50; /27 only gives 30.

questions.question: Which single prefix summarizes 192.168.0.0/24 and 192.168.1.0/24?
questions.explication: The two networks share their first 23 bits: 192.168.0.0/23 covers .0.0 to .1.255.

questions.question: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explication: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long and written in hexadecimal.

questions.question: What is a hextet?
choix: A 6-bit segment of the interface ID
questions.explication: Hextet is the unofficial term for a 16-bit segment, i.e. four hexadecimal values.

questions.question: Which statement about IPv6 address case is true?
choix: They must be written in uppercase
They must be written in lowercase
questions.explication: IPv6 addresses are not case-sensitive and can be written in lowercase or uppercase.

questions.question: Applying the leading-zero rule, how is 0a00 written?
questions.explication: Only leading zeros are removed; trailing zeros must stay, otherwise the address would be ambiguous.

questions.question: What is the compressed form of 2001:0db8:0000:1111:0000:0000:0000:0200?
questions.explication: Remove leading zeros, then replace the run of three zero hextets by '::'.

questions.question: How many times can '::' appear in one IPv6 address?
questions.explication: The double colon can only be used once, otherwise several addresses would be possible.

questions.question: Which is the correct compression of 2001:0db8:0000:00a3:abcd:0000:0000:1234?
questions.explication: '::' replaces the longest run (two hextets); the single zero hextet stays '0'.

questions.question: Which address type does IPv6 NOT have?
questions.explication: IPv6 has no broadcast; the all-nodes multicast address gives essentially the same result.

questions.question: Where is a packet sent to an IPv6 anycast address delivered?
choix: To the device with the lowest MAC address
To all of the devices on the local link
To every device sharing that same address
To the nearest device having that address
questions.explication: An anycast address is a unicast address assigned to several devices; packets are routed to the nearest one.

questions.question: What prefix length is recommended for IPv6 LANs?
questions.explication: The recommended prefix length for LANs and most networks is /64, because SLAAC uses 64 bits for the interface ID.

questions.question: Which IPv6 address is similar to a public IPv4 address?
questions.explication: GUAs are globally unique, internet-routable addresses, like public IPv4 addresses.

questions.question: Which range are GUAs currently assigned from?
questions.explication: Only GUAs with first bits 001 (2000::/3) are assigned; they start with 2 or 3.

questions.question: Which range are IPv6 link-local addresses in?
questions.explication: LLAs are in the fe80::/10 range.

questions.question: Which statement about IPv6 link-local addresses is true?
choix: They cannot be routed off the link
They are assigned by the ISP
They are optional on an interface
questions.explication: Packets with a source or destination LLA cannot be routed. Every IPv6 interface must have one.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a GUA?
choix: Vendor code, serial number and routing prefix
Area ID, router ID and the interface number
Global routing prefix, subnet ID, interface ID
Network ID, host ID and destination port number
questions.explication: Global routing prefix (from the ISP) + subnet ID (the organization's subnets) + interface ID (host part).

questions.question: Which GUA field is equivalent to the host portion of an IPv4 address?
questions.explication: The interface ID is equivalent to the host portion of an IPv4 address.

questions.question: What is the IPv6 all-zeros host address reserved for?
choix: The loopback address of the host
The default gateway of the subnet
questions.explication: The all-0s address is reserved as a Subnet-Router anycast address and should be assigned only to routers.

questions.question: What is the best practice for a host's IPv6 default gateway?
questions.explication: The router's GUA or LLA can be used; best practice is to use the LLA.

questions.question: Which Cisco command configures an IPv6 GUA on an interface?
questions.explication: The command is ipv6 address ipv6-address/prefix-length; IPv6 commands mostly replace ip with ipv6.

questions.question: Which message does a host send to discover IPv6 routers?
questions.explication: Hosts send ICMPv6 RS messages; routers answer with RA messages.

questions.question: Which protocol carries RS and RA messages?
questions.explication: Devices obtain GUAs dynamically through ICMPv6 messages (RS and RA).

questions.question: With SLAAC, where does the device get its prefix?
questions.explication: With SLAAC the prefix comes from the RA; the device builds its interface ID with EUI-64 or randomly.

questions.question: With 'SLAAC and stateless DHCPv6', what does the DHCPv6 server provide?
choix: The GUA of the host and its prefix length
The interface ID that the host has to use
Other information such as DNS and domain name
The default gateway address of the subnet
questions.explication: The device creates its GUA with SLAAC; the stateless DHCPv6 server only gives extra information such as DNS.
questions.piege: Only STATEFUL DHCPv6 assigns the GUA itself.

questions.question: Which RA method is most similar to DHCP for IPv4?
questions.explication: With stateful DHCPv6 the server gives the GUA, prefix length, DNS and other information, like DHCPv4.

questions.question: What value is inserted in the middle of the MAC address by EUI-64?
questions.explication: EUI-64 inserts the 16-bit value fffe in the middle of the 48-bit MAC address.

questions.question: What is the EUI-64 interface ID of MAC fc:99:47:75:ce:e0?
questions.explication: Insert fffe in the middle, then flip the 7th bit: fc (11111100) becomes fe (11111110).
questions.piege: Do not forget to flip the 7th bit of the first byte.

questions.question: Which bit of the MAC address does EUI-64 reverse?
questions.explication: The 7th bit of the client MAC address is reversed from 0 to 1.

questions.question: What is Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) used for?
choix: Converting a MAC into an interface ID
Finding the router on the link
Checking an IPv6 address is unique
questions.explication: DAD is similar to an ARP request for its own address: if there is no reply, the address is unique.

questions.question: Since Windows Vista, how does Windows create its IPv6 interface ID?
questions.explication: Beginning with Windows Vista, Windows uses a randomly generated interface ID instead of EUI-64.

questions.question: What is the prefix of IPv6 multicast addresses?
questions.explication: IPv6 multicast addresses have the prefix ff00::/8.

questions.question: Which multicast group do all IPv6 routers join?
questions.explication: ff02::1 = all-nodes group; ff02::2 = all-routers group.

questions.question: Which address gives the same result as an IPv4 broadcast?
questions.explication: The all-nodes multicast group ff02::1 is received by every IPv6 interface on the link.

questions.question: Which statement about IPv6 multicast addresses is true?
choix: They are always confined to the local link
They can only be destination addresses
They always start with the fe80 prefix
They can only be used as source addresses
questions.explication: Multicast addresses can only be destination addresses, never source addresses.

questions.question: With a /48 global routing prefix and a 16-bit subnet ID, how many /64 subnets are possible?
questions.explication: 16 subnet-ID bits: 2^16 = 65,536 /64 subnets.

questions.question: How do you create successive IPv6 subnets from 2001:db8:acad::/48?
choix: Borrow bits from the interface ID
questions.explication: Only the subnet ID hextet is incremented in hexadecimal; the global routing prefix stays the same.

questions.question: Which transition technique carries an IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet?
questions.explication: Tunneling encapsulates IPv6 inside IPv4. Dual stack runs both stacks; NAT64 translates.

questions.question: A device runs IPv4 and IPv6 protocol stacks at the same time. What is this called?
questions.explication: Dual stack: devices run both IPv4 and IPv6 stacks simultaneously.

questions.question: When does a Cisco router automatically create an IPv6 LLA on an interface?
choix: When a GUA is assigned to it
When the interface is shut down
questions.explication: Cisco routers automatically create an LLA (with EUI-64 by default) whenever a GUA is assigned to the interface.

questions.question: Which standard documents the Spanning Tree Protocol?
questions.explication: STP is documented in IEEE 802.1D. 802.1Q is VLAN tagging; RFC 2328 is OSPF.

questions.question: What is the purpose of STP?
choix: Giving an IP address to each switch of the LAN
Choosing the best Layer 3 route between networks
Pruning a switched topology into a loop-free tree
Tagging every frame with its VLAN identifier
questions.explication: STP dynamically prunes an arbitrary topology of Layer 2 switches into a spanning tree without loops.

questions.question: How is the STP root bridge elected?
questions.explication: In the slides' example: 'Lowest Bridge ID Wins!'.

questions.question: On a non-root bridge, which port becomes the root port?
choix: The port with the highest cost to the root
The port with the most stations
The port with the lowest cost to the root
The port with the highest number
questions.explication: Bridges compute their lowest-cost path to the root bridge; that port is the root port.

questions.question: What happens to ports that are neither root ports nor designated ports?
questions.explication: Redundant ports are blocked; a blocked port can move to forwarding if the topology changes.

questions.question: What do bridges send when bridge ports change state?
questions.explication: Bridges send topology change notification BPDUs when bridge ports change state.

questions.question: What does PortFast do?
choix: Moves an edge port straight to forwarding
Raises the speed of the trunk port links
Blocks any port on which a BPDU is received
Tags the frames with VLAN information
questions.explication: Edge ports configured with PortFast transition directly to forwarding, without lingering in discarding and learning.

questions.question: What does BPDU Guard do?
choix: Encrypts the BPDUs exchanged by switches
Turns an access port into a trunk port
Shuts a PortFast port that receives a BPDU
Elects the root bridge faster than plain STP
questions.explication: BPDU Guard shuts down a PortFast-enabled port if a BPDU from another switch is received.

questions.question: Why do designers use VLANs?
choix: To give MAC addresses to hosts
questions.explication: Designers use VLANs to constrain broadcast traffic, so a faulty NIC cannot flood the whole domain.

questions.question: What is added to a frame leaving a switch on a trunk link?
choix: A VLAN tag with a VLAN identifier
An IP header with the VLAN subnet
A TCP header with a port number
questions.explication: A special header, the VLAN tag, is added; it contains the VLAN ID the frame belongs to.

questions.question: Which VLAN tagging protocol is proprietary to Cisco?
questions.explication: Inter-Switch Link (ISL) is proprietary and should be ignored unless old Cisco switches lack 802.1Q.

questions.question: What does Cisco's VTP do?
choix: Elects the root bridge of the tree
Tags each frame with its VLAN ID
questions.explication: VTP is a switch-to-switch and switch-to-router management protocol that exchanges VLAN configuration changes.

questions.question: Which DTP combination should be avoided?
choix: Trunk on one side and trunk on the other side
Off on both sides of the link between switches
Desirable on both of the sides of the link
Nonegotiate on one side, auto on the other
questions.explication: Nonegotiate + off and nonegotiate + auto result in an 802.1Q mode mismatch.

questions.question: What does the Cisco Dynamic Trunk Protocol (DTP) negotiate?
choix: The IP address of the switch
questions.explication: DTP lets a switch negotiate with the remote side to enable or disable 802.1Q.

questions.question: Where are interior routing protocols used?
questions.explication: Interior protocols are used within an AS; exterior protocols between ASes.

questions.question: Which is a definition of an autonomous system?
choix: A switch that runs the Spanning Tree Protocol
A host configured with a static IP address
A router with its own redundant power supply
questions.explication: An AS is a network or set of networks under the administrative control of a single entity.

questions.question: Which factor is NOT used by routing protocols to determine the best route?
questions.explication: Metrics in the course: bandwidth, delay, load, reliability, hop count, cost. Redundancy is not one.

questions.question: Which metric measures the number of routers a packet goes through?
questions.explication: Hop count = number of routers a packet must travel through before reaching the destination network.

questions.question: What can happen when routing protocols converge slowly?
questions.explication: Routing algorithms that converge slowly can cause routing loops or network outages.

questions.question: What is convergence?
choix: Merging two separate networks into one
All routers agreeing on optimal routes
Joining two VLANs on the same switch
questions.explication: Convergence is the process of agreement, by all routers, on optimal routes.

questions.question: How does a distance-vector router share its routing information?
choix: It sends LSAs only when a link changes
It floods its topology database once
It waits for neighbours to ask for it
It periodically broadcasts its whole table
questions.explication: A distance-vector router transmits its routing table periodically (e.g. every 30 s) via broadcast.

questions.question: When do link-state routers send updates?
choix: Only when there is a change
questions.explication: Link-state routers send updates only when there is a change, as link-state advertisements (LSAs).

questions.question: Which algorithm do link-state protocols apply to find shortest paths?
questions.explication: Link-state algorithms apply Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on their graph of the internetwork.

questions.question: How do link-state algorithms view the internetwork?
questions.explication: Distance-vector algorithms keep a list; link-state algorithms think of the internetwork as a graph.

questions.question: Which of the following routing protocols is NOT classless?
questions.explication: RIP (v1) and IGRP are classful; RIPv2, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS and BGP are classless.

questions.question: What do classful routing protocols NOT include in route advertisements?
questions.explication: Classful protocols do not include the subnet mask; consistency of masks is assumed.

questions.question: What is RIP's metric?
questions.explication: RIP uses a single routing metric, hop count.

questions.question: What is RIP's maximum hop count?
questions.explication: RIP's maximum hop count is 15; IGRP raised it to 255.

questions.question: How often does RIP broadcast its routing table?
questions.explication: RIP broadcasts its routing table every 30 seconds, 25 routes per packet.

questions.question: Which feature does RIPv2 add to RIP?
choix: It raises the hop limit up to 255 hops
It uses a composite bandwidth metric
It runs Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph
It includes the subnet mask in updates
questions.explication: RIPv2 includes the subnet mask (prefix routing, VLSM) and simple authentication.

questions.question: What is the most significant improvement of IGRP over RIP?
questions.explication: IGRP solved RIP's 15-hop limit (255 hops), its single metric and its 30 s timer (90 s).
questions.piege: 30 s timer, single metric and broadcasting every 30 s describe RIP itself.

questions.question: Which values does IGRP combine into a composite metric?
choix: Cost and the AS path list
questions.explication: IGRP combines values for bandwidth, load and delay to create a composite metric.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an EIGRP improvement listed in the course?
choix: Incremental updates with only the changes
Fast adjustment to changes in the internetwork
A metric representing the cost of a given path
questions.explication: A metric representing the cost of a path describes link-state protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS.

questions.question: How many bits does the EIGRP metric use?
questions.explication: EIGRP uses the same metric as IGRP with more granularity: 32 bits instead of 24.

questions.question: Which protocols allow unequal-cost load balancing?
questions.explication: If IGRP or Enhanced IGRP routing is used, unequal-cost load balancing is possible.

questions.question: In OSPF, which cost value makes a path preferred?
questions.explication: The lower the cost, the more likely the interface is used to forward traffic.

questions.question: What is the default OSPF cost of a 100 Mbit/s interface on a Cisco router?
What is the default OSPF cost of a 10 Mbit/s Ethernet interface on a Cisco router?
Which RFC defines OSPF?
questions.explication: OSPF is an open standard defined in RFC 2328. RFC 1878 lists subnet masks.

questions.question: What is the name of the OSPF central backbone?
questions.explication: OSPF has a central backbone (Area Zero) that physically attaches all other areas through ABRs.

questions.question: Compared to OSPF, IS-IS is described as all of these EXCEPT:
questions.explication: IS-IS is similar to OSPF but somewhat more flexible, efficient and scalable.

questions.question: Who designed IS-IS?
questions.explication: IS-IS was designed by the ISO for the OSI protocols; Integrated IS-IS also handles IP.

questions.question: In IS-IS, which routers route between areas?
questions.explication: Level 1 routers route within an area; Level 2 routers route between areas and form the backbone.

questions.question: Which statement concerning BGP is true?
choix: It transmits an ordered list of autonomous systems
It extends its backbone by adding Level 2 routers
It combines bandwidth, load and delay into one metric
It uses hop count with a maximum value of 15 hops
questions.explication: BGP is a distance-vector protocol but transmits an ordered list of ASes rather than a hop count.
questions.piege: The other options describe IGRP, RIP and IS-IS.

questions.question: Which protocol is usually considered an exterior routing protocol?
questions.explication: BGP is used on the Internet among large ISPs and major companies, between autonomous systems.

questions.question: Which protocol keeps neighbours' routing tables to use as feasible successors?
questions.explication: EIGRP keeps track of neighbours' routing tables and uses them as feasible successors.

questions.question: What tool helps match routing protocols to a customer's goals?
questions.explication: A decision table matches protocols to the customer's critical goals and other goals.

questions.question: Which transport protocol supports reliability?
questions.explication: TCP supports reliability while UDP doesn't.

questions.question: How many bytes of overhead does the TCP header add?
questions.explication: TCP adds 20 bytes of overhead; UDP only 8 bytes.

questions.question: How many bytes of overhead does the UDP header add?
questions.explication: UDP adds only 8 bytes of overhead.

questions.question: What are the pieces of communication in UDP called?
questions.explication: The pieces of communication in UDP are called datagrams.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three TCP reliability operations?
questions.explication: TCP reliability relies on numbering/tracking segments, acknowledging data and retransmitting unacknowledged data.

questions.question: Which TCP flag is used to terminate a connection?
questions.explication: When a side has no more data to send, it sends a segment with the FIN flag set.

questions.question: How many steps does the TCP connection establishment take?
questions.explication: TCP connections are established with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).

questions.question: What does the TCP window size field indicate?
choix: Total size of the TCP header in bytes
Bytes the receiver can accept at once
Number of segments that were already sent
Time to wait before a retransmission
questions.explication: The window size is the number of bytes the destination can accept and process at one time.

questions.question: How is the TCP initial sequence number (ISN) chosen?
questions.explication: The ISN is randomly chosen during setup, then incremented by the number of transmitted bytes.

questions.question: Which application is better suited to UDP?
questions.explication: Live audio/video and VoIP tolerate some loss but need little delay: UDP. Email, web and databases use TCP.

questions.question: Which pair of applications are simple request/reply applications using UDP?
questions.explication: DNS and DHCP are simple request and reply applications that use UDP.

questions.question: In UDP, what port does the client use as source port?
choix: The same as the destination port
questions.explication: The UDP client process dynamically selects a source port; the destination is the server's well-known port.

questions.question: The TCP/IP application layer performs the functions of which OSI layers?
questions.explication: The TCP/IP application layer covers OSI application, presentation and session layers.

questions.question: In a peer-to-peer network, which statement is true?
choix: A dedicated server is always required
Each peer can act as client and server
Only one device can be a server
questions.explication: In P2P, every peer can function as both server and client; roles are set per request.

questions.question: Which port does an SMTP client connect to?
questions.explication: An SMTP client sends an email by connecting to an SMTP server on port 25.

questions.question: Which TCP port do POP requests use?
questions.explication: Email clients direct their POP requests to mail servers on TCP port 110.

questions.question: Which email protocol keeps messages on the server until the user deletes them?
questions.explication: With IMAP, originals stay on the server; POP downloads messages and removes them from the server.

questions.question: Which TCP port does FTP use for control traffic?
questions.explication: The client opens the control connection on TCP port 21 and the data connection on TCP port 20.

questions.question: How many connections does FTP require between client and server?
questions.explication: FTP needs one connection for commands and replies, and another for the actual file transfer.

questions.question: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
choix: Faster loading of the web pages
A second data connection for files
questions.explication: HTTP is not secure; HTTPS uses authentication and encryption to secure data.

questions.question: Which HTTP request does a browser send to get a web page?
questions.explication: The browser sends a GET request to the server's IP address and asks for the file.
